html:
Behavioral capabilities

Between 6 and 12 months, infants flip from mostly reactive observers to self-propelled epistemic foragers, with capability ramping across motor, manual, social-communicative, and problem-solving domains.

Median hands-and-knees crawling lands near 8.3 months, cruising and brief supported steps cluster around 9-10 months, and the window for independent walking is strikingly wide (roughly the 1st-99th percentiles span  8.2 to 17.6 months) so experience, not a fixed schedule, determines the timeline 1, 2, 3, 4. Locomotion rapidly becomes calibrated to environmental affordances: crawlers vs. novice walkers learn posture-specific "can/can’t" boundaries (e.g., which slopes are safely descendable), with famously poor transfer when switching from crawling to walking, and errorful exploration that reflects active estimation of action limits rather than mere clumsiness 5, 6. Similarly, many experienced crawlers begin to show wariness of heights (hesitation/avoidance and/or cautious exploration) on drop-off paradigms 7, 8. Self-produced locomotion also enables landmark-based spatial orientation and spatial updating: across 6-12 months infants increasingly remember where an object is relative to stable cues in the environment (basic relational landmark use), supporting search and reorientation in a way that goes beyond egocentric reach space 9.

Grasp pre-shaping (adjusting to object shape) and timing (hand closure) become reliable by 12 months 10. Grasping strategies move from whole-hand grasps to an emerging pincer grasp (ability to use the index finger and thumb only) with voluntary release and basic bimanual coordination (typically evident around 7-9 months 11), expanding the space of self-produced object contingencies the brain can sample. These gains unlock constructive, compositional object play: late in this window infants increasingly stack, nest, and affix (join/attach) objects, creating repeatable "part/whole + spatial-relation" scenes that the world model can encode as structured states rather than single-object snapshots 12 (one study, however, estimates that only 15% of 10-month-olds can stack one block on another 13). Meanwhile, infants’ percussive "banging" becomes straighter and more force-controlled from across this window, a motor trajectory that may scaffold simple tool use near the end of this period 14; near the end of this window, infants begin to acquire proto-tool-use policies under favorable geometries (e.g., early success with rake-like tools when tool-target contiguity is high) 15 but remain largely unable to learn conventional artifact actions by observation (copying demonstrated functional uses of novel objects) 16, 17, despite basic delayed imitation being possible before this window. A 2026 observational study examines children’s object engagement (Figure) 125. The study compares material engagement across early childhood (Figure).

On the perceptual side, the visual system undergoes a qualitative computational shift during this window: whereas 3-4-month-olds can detect subtle image-level luminance changes (due to illumination shifts) that are not salient to adults, this "pre-constancy" sensitivity fades by ∼5 months and is replaced, by ∼7-8 months, with perceptual constancy for surface color and material–the ability to perceive stable distal surface properties despite dynamic variation in the retinal image across viewpoints and illuminations 18. Unlike size and shape constancy (present at birth), surface-property constancy thus appears to require postnatal calibration, and its emergence implies that object representations increasingly encode distal surfaces rather than proximal images. Similarly, categories become more selective and knowledge-structured across this window: in general, categories increasingly reflect relations among features (e.g., correlations/co-occurrences) and abstraction of invariant structure (e.g dogs have four legs and distinct noses) rather than treating features as independent 19. By ∼\sim7-11 months, object-examination paradigms reveal differentiation of broad conceptual domains such as animals vs. vehicles (often with domain-specific substructure, e.g airplanes vs. cars vs. motorcycles) 20, and by ∼\sim10-11 months infants can show knowledge-based category discrimination that is not well-explained as an ad hoc response to perceptual similarity alone 21. These categories begin to support inductive inference and object identity tracking. By ∼\sim9 months, infants use minimal experience with a single exemplar to draw simple inferences about nonobvious properties (e.g whether an object will float) of novel objects, and these expectations reliably guide exploratory play 22. Relatedly, 9-11 month-olds can generalize demonstrated properties preferentially within appropriate domains (e.g., animal-appropriate vs. vehicle-appropriate behaviors) 23, 24. Moreover, object-individuation paradigms (where multiple objects that are in contact must be segmented suggest a transition between ∼\sim10 and 12 months: infants increasingly use object kind/property information to individuate, going beyond spatiotemporal cues (i.e objects moving independently) 25, 26; this is further supported by evidence from manual-search paradigms, where 10-12-month-olds are able to determine whether "one vs. two objects" are inside a container 27. Awake infant fMRI now shows animacy-based organization emerging across the first year while lateral object-selective cortex matures later (Figure) 123. Awake infant fMRI now shows animacy-based organization emerging across the first year while lateral object-selective cortex matures later (Figure).

On the communication front, production advances from canonical babbling (repetitive, speech-like syllables, such as "ba-ba" or "ma-ma") toward the first words 28, 29, 30, and the amount and quality of canonical syllables already forecast later language outcomes. Receptive language is, however, not waiting for production: 6-9-month-olds recognize everyday words in natural scenes 31, and English-learning infants begin segmenting words from fluent speech by  7.5 months 32, leveraging additional segmentation cues by  10.5 months 33, 34. By ∼\sim12 months, infants can also resolve referential ambiguity via cross-situational statistics: when individual naming events are ambiguous (multiple objects present), they track word-object co-occurrence regularities across events to identify the correct referent 35. In parallel, the perceptual front end specializes as non-native phonetic contrasts that 6-month-olds hear often fade by 10-12 months 36, while native categories strengthen 28. This experience-driven narrowing is not unique to speech: face-processing systems undergo a parallel contraction, with 6-month-olds able to discriminate individual faces of other species (e.g., monkeys) but 9-month-olds no longer able to do so unless given intervening individuation training 37, suggesting a domain-general mechanism that prunes representational distinctions not reinforced by environmental statistics. A 2025 study compares infant vocalizations in different play contexts (Figure) 126. The study also examines infant responses to caregivers (Figure).

Social cognition becomes increasingly triadic (include self, other, and a shared referent (an object, event, or location in the environment)) and informational: by 10-11 months infants follow gaze selectively when others can see (eyes open) 38, and around 12 months many point declaratively to share information, along with making requests 39, 40; pointing is considered a landmark communication skill of the 12-month mark 41, 42. 43. Around the first birthday, pointing can also function as an epistemic request–a way to solicit new information from an adult about an ambiguous referent, not just to share attention or request objects 44. Another key instance of triadic communication, social referencing becomes a portable, modality-flexible uncertainty resolver. As locomotion and manual exploration make more situations genuinely risky or ambiguous, infants increasingly query caregivers’ affect to set the valence/expected value of a novel referent and to gate approach vs. avoidance policies. In the classic visual-cliff paradigm, 12-month-olds use maternal emotional messages to decide whether to cross an apparent drop-off (positive signals promote crossing; fearful signals sharply suppress it), demonstrating affect-to-action regulation rather than mere mood contagion 45. In "ambiguous toy" paradigms, 10-13-month-olds’ looks to the parent predict systematic shifts in exploration/withdrawal, consistent with a multi-component skill (referential looking →\rightarrow appraisal →\rightarrow behavior regulation) that consolidates across the first year 46. Unlike the previous window, by ∼\sim12 months the appraisal no longer requires rich intersensory redundancy: infants can use face-only or voice-only emotional information to regulate behavior toward a novel stimulus, with vocal fear sufficient to suppress approach even in the absence of facial cues 47, 48. Social-emotional signals also start acting like value tags that persist beyond the immediate moment: 11-month-olds show delayed regulatory effects of an adult’s emotional display on later behavior toward the referent, implying that social referencing is beginning to write longer-lived affective priors into the world model 49. Referencing is not strictly mother-bound: 1-year-olds can use affect from another (familiarized) adult to guide their response to a novel object even when the mother is present but neutral, broadening the class of "informants" whose appraisals can train action selection 50. A longitudinal study tracks early bids for joint attention (Figure) 127. An experiment tests object encoding during joint attention (Figure). The authors also report bids at each assessment (Figure). The experiment measures infants’ looking behavior (Figure).

Social cognition also becomes more recursive: whereas 5-month-olds uniformly prefer individuals who act positively toward others regardless of the target’s moral status, by ∼\sim8 months infants selectively prefer characters who act positively toward prosocial individuals and characters who act negatively toward antisocial individuals. This implies that the agent model now composes at least two layers of social evaluation–tracking both a target’s prior behavior and a second agent’s response to that target–yielding rudimentary second-order social judgment 51. Relatedly, by ∼\sim9 months, infants react with greater impatience when an adult is unwilling to hand over a toy than when the adult is unable to do so (e.g., clumsy or physically blocked), further indicating that the world model parses others’ behavior in terms of underlying intentions and dispositions 52. Intention/action understanding also becomes motor-grounded and predictive: by ∼12 months (but not 6 months), infants watching another person reach for an object shift their gaze to the reach target before the hand arrives, and this anticipatory looking correlates with the infant’s own ability to perform the same action 53. This suggests that by the end of the first year, the observer internally simulates the actor’s movement plan via a shared motor forward model to generate goal predictions–linking the infant’s own visuomotor experience to the prediction of others’ behavior. Perhaps most strikingly, the "agent model" begins tracking not just what others intend, but what others know or have experienced. By 12 months, infants track whether an adult was present or absent during an object’s introduction; if the adult was absent, the infant’s world model treats the object as "new" for the adult and will selectively offer or point to that object over familiar ones 54. Even earlier, by 7 months, looking-time paradigms indicate that infants automatically encode another agent’s belief about an object’s hidden location, showing altered reaction times when the agent’s belief conflicts with physical reality 55. This implies a profound architectural upgrade: the infant’s world model now maintains parallel, decoupled state representations–the actual state of the world, and the state of the world as represented within another agent’s internal model. The criteria for classifying an entity as an "agent" also become less tied to morphological cues and more sensitive to behavioral structure. While early in life infants are strongly biased by cues such as face-like configurations and biological motion, by the end of the first year they can attribute goal-directedness and attentional orientation to morphologically unfamiliar, even faceless objects on the basis of cues such as contingent interaction and organized, environment-directed behavior. In classic studies, infants treated an unfamiliar object that had interacted contingently and behaved intentionally as goal-directed, and they also followed the subsequent orientation of non-human faceless agents after contingent interaction, suggesting that temporal contingency and behavioral reciprocity can serve as powerful triggers for instantiating an agent model even in the absence of recognizable biological form 56, 57, 58, 59.

A foundational action-coupled advance is the onset of manual search for fully hidden objects at∼\sim8 months: infants now lift a cloth or reach behind a screen to retrieve a completely invisible object, implying that the world model maintains a spatial representation of the hidden object sufficient to guide goal-directed action toward it–bridging the gap between the looking-time evidence for object permanence measurable months earlier and its expression through the motor system 60, 61. Likewise, performance on A-not-B (where infants mistakenly search for a hidden object in a familiar location (A) rather than a new location (B), even after witnessing the object being moved to B) improves though perseveration (repetitive failures) is common across this window 62. 7-9-month-olds also increasingly solve one-step means-end problems (e.g., pulling a cloth to retrieve a distant object) 63, and 9-12-month-olds exhibit deferred imitation after 24-hour delays (which is quite rare for 6-month-olds 64)–an early readout of long-term recall 65. Importantly, deferred imitation becomes increasingly decontextualized: whereas 6-month-olds’ deferred imitation is tightly bound to the specific demonstration context, experimenter, and stimulus objects, by ∼12 months infants generalize imitated action sequences across changes in background context, demonstrator identity, and object exemplar 66, 67, reflecting a shift from episode-locked to more abstract, transferable event representations that can support flexible reuse. Infants’ working memory updating + inhibitory control improves across 9-12 months (visible in reduced perseveration on A-not-B-like demands), and visual working memory shows a marked capacity increase across this window (often reported as rising from  1 item earlier in infancy toward  3 items by  10-12 months in change-detection paradigms) 68, 69, 70, 71. A study presents infants with expected and unexpected physical events (Figure) 130. The study measures differences in infants’ looking preferences (Figure).

Core physical priors also sharpen: infants refine rule-like expectations about physical support across this window (i.e accurately predicting how much physical overlap is needed for stability, related to block stacking) 72, 73, 74, 75, and their approximate number system also increases in precision–from discriminating 1:2 ratios at  6 months to  2:3 by ∼\sim9-10 months–yielding quantifiable gains in representational acuity 76. Exploration also sharpens: by∼\sim9 months, infants finger textured objects more than nontextured ones, shake or bang sounding objects more than nonsounding ones, and press pliable objects more than nonpliable ones 77; by ∼11 months, expectation violation does not merely elicit longer looking–it drives targeted hypothesis-testing exploration. Infants who witness a solidity violation (an object appearing to pass through a wall) selectively bang the object against a surface, while those who witness a support violation (an object appearing to hover in mid-air) selectively drop it, as if testing the specific physical property that was violated. Moreover, infants learn novel information (e.g., a hidden squeaker) about expectation-violating objects better than about objects that behaved predictably 78. This implies that the world model generates structured prediction errors that specify what needs updating, and that exploration is recruited as a corrective inference mechanism rather than an undirected response to surprise. Infants also begin exploring containment and insertion by the end of the first year 79, 80, 81. More generally, by 11 months, after experience with a novel object, infants can transfer their exploration skills to objects with the same novel properties 82, meaning core physical representations are beginning to crystallize in a disentangled form (in contrast to the 3-6 months window, where core physical priors often fail to generalize 83, 84). Causal reasoning also extends beyond observable events: by 10-12 months, infants who see a beanbag emerge from behind a screen on a self-propelled-looking trajectory infer the existence of a hidden agent behind the screen as the plausible cause–expecting to find an agent (i.e a hand or even a puppet 85) when the screen is removed and looking longer when no agent is present. Importantly, this inference is selective: infants draw it when the object’s motion is consistent with having been launched by an agent but not when the object is self-propelled 86, and use the beanbag’s trajectory to predict the position of a hand, but not a toy block 85.

In sequence-learning paradigms, while 6-month-olds show a preference for novel spatiotemporal sequences containing basic patterns (e.g., stimuli alternating between left and right locations), 11-month-olds show a distinct preference for more complex sequences (e.g those defined by shape/color differences) 87. In general, sequence learning becomes more abstract and relational across this window. By 8-11 months, infants can generalize certain repetition-based visual rules across novel items (with younger infants succeeding on simpler repetition structures and older infants on harder position-sensitive contrasts), and by ∼\sim11 months they detect reversals in ordinal numerical direction (ascending vs. descending numerosities), indicating that the world model is beginning to encode higher-order structure over sequences rather than only local transitions or feature co-occurrences 88, 89. Similarly, by ∼\sim9 months, infants can also learn statistical structure from passive observation of complex scenes: after exposure to many multi-element displays, they attend more to feature pairs that are not only more frequent co-occurrences but also more predictive (higher conditional probability), implying that the world model is estimating structured joint/conditional statistics over compositional visual features–not merely learning isolated associations 90; this can be seen as the scene-level expression of the aforementioned advancements in object categorization. A longitudinal experiment tests visual statistical learning (Figure) 128. The study compares an EEG learning index across ages (Figure).

Training data and optimization

The onset of self-produced locomotion has been characterized as a developmental cascade that simultaneously reorganizes spatial coding, social referencing, wariness of heights, and aspects of object search–not because crawling directly causes each change, but because it exposes the infant to a qualitatively new distribution of self-generated experience with distance, occlusion, spatial perspective shifts, and the need for distal social-emotional information 91.

By ∼\sim9 months, joint attention does not merely redirect looking; it selectively changes how objects are encoded. Infants remember different–and behaviorally more useful–properties of a novel object when it is introduced under eye contact / shared attention than when the same object is encountered in a noncommunicative parallel-attention context, indicating that the world model is beginning to treat socially cued objects as privileged learning targets rather than as ordinary scene items 92, 93, 94.

Near the end of the first year, labels begin to actively reorganize object representations rather than merely accompany them. Words (but not matched nonlinguistic tones) facilitate category formation, and by ∼\sim12 months infants can use referential labeling cues to decide whether a scene should be represented as containing one object or two, indicating that linguistic signals are beginning to constrain both category structure and object individuation inside the world model 95, 96.

Explanation-based learning in infancy

Do words facilitate object categorization in 9-month-old infants?

The infant now becomes a prolific generator of its own training data.

A major driver is the embodiment shift: new postures (sitting -> crawling -> cruising) change the mapping between optic flow, vestibular cues, and motor commands, so affordance knowledge is elaborated on in a posture-specific way; locomotion plus posture control let infants generate rich optic-flow/vestibular/proprioceptive tuples on demand, while egocentric studies show that everyday learning episodes are engineered into single-object, centered views dominated by hands (often because adults place and hold targets in the infant’s field), effectively reducing referential uncertainty during naming or demonstration. Manual exploration supplies dense cause-effect samples: banging, shaking, mouthing, throwing, and two-handed manipulation produce repeatable audiovisual-haptic contingencies, with stabilized sitting and the emergence of the pincer grasp (using the thumb and index finger to grasp small objects) turbocharging visual-manual exploration: rotating, transferring, and dropping objects couples haptics with vision and, empirically, is when 3D object completion comes online 99–evidence that manipulation experience is a key aspect of the curriculum for viewpoint-invariant object models. A longitudinal study records infant movement and vocalization (Figure) 124. The study examines movement around vocalization onset (Figure).

Exploration is not random: attention follows a "Goldilocks" policy that prefers stimuli of intermediate predictive complexity (demonstrated in 7- and 8-month-olds 100), and violations of expectation at  11 months trigger hypothesis-testing play and faster learning–an intrinsic surprise-weighted sampler that concentrates updates where gradients are steep.

The vocal system runs a parallel closed-loop generator: on top of producing auditory prediction errors, canonical babbling recruits contingent caregiver feedback that immediately reshapes infant syllable statistics toward speech-like forms, a social reinforcement signal that alters both produced and heard distributions. A study combines movement sensors and vocal recordings (Figure). The researchers examine the timing of infant motion and vocalization (Figure).

High-precision supervision comes from joint attention and ostension: "follow-in" labeling when the child already fixates on the physical referent predicts vocabulary growth (especially when paired with "motionese" demonstrations), and by  12 months, gaze following and attention to a talker’s mouth predict later productive vocabulary; these are all powerful cross-modal alignment signals that accelerate learning.

Sleep acts as a periodic batch processor for the day’s episodes: a ≥30-min nap within  4 hours preserves novel action memories in 6- and 12-month-olds, and between 9 and 16 months, sleep reorganizes specific word-object traces into more abstract, category-like knowledge.

Finally, caregiver-infant biobehavioral synchrony (especially affectionate touch) stabilizes arousal and vagal tone, effectively gating learning rates during play and teaching bouts. Caregivers also gate whether certain (especially dangerous) states are even sampled, avoiding disaster and overall shaping which parts of the environment enter memory.

Optimization

The internal optimizers now lock to the statistics of a much richer sensorimotor and social world.

Cerebellar microcomplexes run high-bandwidth supervised calibration on the rapidly expanding motor repertoire: they calibrate timing and gain for head-trunk stabilization, smooth pursuit during active gaze shifts, visually guided reaching and the emerging pincer grasp, and the first locomotor primitives (belly crawl -> hands-and-knees -> cruising). Climbing-fiber bursts remain the essential, precisely routed teacher, but their "analog" character now matters: larger retinal slip, reach endpoint error, and footfall mistiming yield bigger complex-spike Ca2+ plateaus and faster step sizes, while context arriving on mossy fibers (posture, target motion, effector used) ensures that updates are feature-selective rather than global. Together, this yields rapid gain and timing corrections for oculomotor and limb controllers that infants visibly acquire across this window.

Concurrently, cortico-striatal actor-critic loops shift from ventral/limbic dominance to stronger dorsomedial recruitment as goal-directed choice emerges; phasic dopamine broadcasts continue to implement a distributional code over returns, which is especially adaptive in this regime because outcomes are both higher variance (novel objects, surfaces, and people) and increasingly long-horizon (multi-step plans like pull-to-stand). Tonic dopamine tracks rising average reward as mobility and social success raise opportunity cost, boosting vigor (latency and force) and biasing the policy toward faster exploration; phasic bursts/dips commit updates only where recent corticostriatal activity laid seconds-long eligibility traces, solving distal credit assignment for multi-step actions like reach-grasp-transfer.

Cortical hierarchies minimize local prediction errors under progressively sharper precision control: feedforward residuals in superficial layers continue to tune invariances for object identity, pose, and occlusion, while apical-tuft feedback carries predictions and plasticity control, opening dendritic plateau-gated plasticity windows when contextual signals warrant; environmentally driven "perceptual narrowing" commits auditory maps to native phonetic contrasts between  6-12 months, while nonnative contrasts decline, a signature of priors sharpening and residuals falling in behaviorally relevant subspaces.

Neuromodulatory controllers arbitrate: acetylcholine up-weights expected-uncertainty terms as cues become reliable (e.g., caregiver vocal prosody or graspable affordances), norepinephrine emits brief mode-switch broadcasts at volatility boundaries (novel places, strangers), and serotonin lengthens the integration window for delayed outcomes, supporting patience and effortful control over longer action chains.

Objectives themselves become more structured: intrinsic reward tracks learning progress (the "Goldilocks" band drives sampling), while triadic joint attention and pedagogical cues (gaze alternation, pointing, infant-directed speech) act as externally supplied goal pointers that label what variables "matter," effectively installing subgoals into OFC/vmPFC state maps and raising the value of information about others’ intentions.

Finally, hippocampal-cortical loops already support sleep-dependent consolidation and generalization: timely naps (≤4 h after learning) stabilize 6- and 12-month-olds’ declarative memories, and spindles relate to infants’ abstraction of word meanings-while canonical slow-oscillation<->spindle coordination is present but still maturing across the first year (with precise ripple coupling better established later), consistent with an offline "compile and train" phase that is functional but not yet adult-like.

Neural development

From 6-12 months, the macroscale picture of the brain tightens along three interacting axes (rhythms, networks, and substrate) and these shifts have clear computational consequences.

Spectrally, infants’ peak-alpha frequency (PAF, the frequency exhibiting maximum power (implicated as a clock on visual temporal processing 101)) continues its climb (meta-analyses put it near  6.1 Hz at 6 months and rising thereafter), and higher PAF within this window already tracks shorter saccadic latencies and sharper temporal attention 102, indicating narrower integration windows for selection and prediction. Beyond alpha, sensorimotor mu/beta activity (which, in adults, is strongly associated with sensorimotor processing and higher-order cognitive tasks 103) becomes more structured, with a low-beta peak emerging by  6 months and mu rhythm gradually accelerating, signals of maturing thalamo-cortical gain control for movement prediction 104, 105. Early gamma responses strengthen as infants maintain multiple occluded objects by  6-8 months 106, 107, 108, foreshadowing faster local assemblies for working memory, while the aperiodic 1/f slope flattens across the first year 109, consistent with evolving excitation-inhibition balance and better throughput. Cross-frequency coordination is still coarse but detectable: slow-oscillation-spindle coupling becomes more systematic between late infancy and toddlerhood 110, laying the scaffolding for hippocampo-cortical credit assignment during sleep even as communication channels continues to mature.

At the network level, higher-order systems that are patchy earlier consolidate into a more segregated-yet-integrated topology. By around one year, the default-mode network shows rapid increases in regional perfusion (delivery of blood, oxygen, and nutrients) that specifically support the emerging DMN 111, 112, marking a nascent internal-modeling system. This system-level refinement sits on a backbone that already exhibits "rich-club"-like organization in infancy 113 and becomes more modular with age, supplying long-range highways for selective exchange while protecting local specialization. Thalamocortical channels (especially pulvinar gateways that gate salience and synchrony) are still tuning but increasingly capable of coordinating cortico-cortical communication essential for selective attention 114 while the frontoparietal control network is quite immature at this stage (and is among the last networks to fully develop) 112. A recent study provides an individualized mapping method for functional networks in young children (Figure) 129. Age-specific network maps include observations from infants 8–10 months old (Figure).

Insert Figure 2 from "Functional Network Development During the First Year: Relative Sequence and Socioeconomic Correlations")

Beneath these dynamics, the physical substrate is racing ahead. White-matter microstructure and myelin-sensitive metrics rise steeply across the first year in major tracts (callosal splenium, optic radiations, corticospinal) 115, 116, 117, and visual/auditory evoked latencies shorten, reflecting faster conduction that supports higher-frequency synchronization and longer-range phase alignment. Synaptically, V1 is in an exuberant state with peak synaptic density roughly between  8-11 months (in line with other primary sensory/motor cortices), while association cortices are still ascending; pruning is increasingly activity- and complement/microglia-mediated 118, 119-mechanistically tying experience statistics and sleep slow waves to circuit sharpening and E/I homeostasis 120, 121. Relative to its size at birth, the 1-year-old’s brain has doubled in volume, largely accounted for by the growth of neural connections in gray matter (i.e., synapse and dendrites), long-range axons, and myelination 122. A clean behavioral readout of these shifts in macroscopic structural properties is "perceptual narrowing": discrimination of non-native phonemes and other-race/other-species faces diminishes as top-down priors strengthen over faster, myelinated pathways-exactly what you’d expect when a broad, exuberant code is being sculpted into an efficient, task-contingent world-model.
